opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core idea behind EgoMimic is that we want to learn from human data at scale. People wear egocentric devices, like the Aria glasses, and just go about their daily tasks: cooking, folding laundry, tidying up. That gives us a huge amount of rich, natural manipulation data that's much cheaper to collect than robot teleoperation.

The catch is the embodiment gap. If your robot looks and moves very differently from a human, then what the model learns from human video doesn't transfer cleanly. The viewpoint is different, the arm reach is different, the way the hands relate to the camera is different. So the policy basically has to learn two separate worlds.

So we flipped the question. Instead of only asking how to make the algorithm bridge a big gap, we asked: why not make the gap smaller in the hardware itself? We put the camera roughly where a person's head would be, and we used the same kind of egocentric sensing. We also set up the arms so their workspace and motion roughly match how human arms move relative to the head. Once the robot sees the world from a similar perspective, and its hands show up in the image in a similar way, human data and robot data start to look like they come from the same distribution. Then you can co-train on both, and the human data actually helps.

There's also a longer-term motivation. Our world is built for human bodies: the counters, the cabinets, the tools. A robot with a roughly human-like form fits into those spaces more naturally. It also lets us use what I think is the most scalable data source we have, which is people simply living their lives. Making the robot more human-like is really about making human experience usable as robot training data.

r001.rationale: The response says a robot that differs greatly from humans makes skills learned from human video transfer poorly, and describes making the robot more human-like to shrink that gap.

fable-5.1.text:
The whole idea behind EgoMimic was that we wanted to learn directly from human video. Humans are the richest source of manipulation data on the planet. You don't have to teleoperate anything, you just put on a pair of glasses and go about your day doing dishes or folding laundry, and now you've got hours of demonstrations. The problem is that if your robot looks nothing like a person, that data is really hard to use. There's this huge embodiment gap. The camera is in a different place, the arms move differently, the hands look different, and the policy has to somehow bridge all of that.

So we tried to shrink that gap as much as we could on the hardware side. We put the camera at roughly head height, looking down at the workspace the way your eyes do when you're working at a table. We used two arms mounted so the kinematics feel similar to shoulders and elbows, and we kept the end effector in roughly the same visual region as a human hand would be. We even masked out the arms and hands in both the human and robot footage so the model sees a scene that looks pretty much the same regardless of who's acting in it.

The reason that matters is that once the observation spaces line up, the human data stops being this separate thing you need a clever transfer trick for. You can essentially treat it as more robot data. We co-train on both, and the human footage gives you diversity in objects, scenes, and motions that would take forever to collect through teleoperation. And we saw real gains from it, especially on generalization to new objects and layouts.

So it wasn't that we wanted a humanoid for its own sake. It was that if you want to tap into the human world as a data source, meeting it halfway with the body is one of the simplest and most effective things you can do.

r001.rationale: The response says a robot unlike a person has an embodiment gap that makes human demonstrations hard to use, and describes making its hardware more human-like to shrink that gap and transfer human data.

astra-6.text:
The motivation is to make it easier for the robot to learn from people. If you watch a person perform a task, their movements are tied to their body—where their arms are, how far they can reach, and how they see the workspace. If the robot has a very different body, translating that demonstration into robot actions becomes harder.

So with EgoMimic, the idea is to bring those closer together. We don’t need the robot to look exactly like a person, but having a more similar arrangement of arms and viewpoint makes human demonstrations more useful. Ultimately, we want people doing everyday tasks to provide a practical source of training data for robots.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a more human-like body makes human demonstrations easier to translate into robot actions, improving learning from human data.

sol-6.1.text: The idea was to make it easier for the robot to learn from people. If you watch someone do a task, their movements are expressed through their body—their arms, their hands, and their viewpoint. When the robot has a similar setup, the connection between what the person does and what the robot should do becomes much more direct. So the goal wasn’t just to make it look human; it was to reduce that gap and make human demonstrations more useful for learning.

r001.rationale: The response says a body similar to a person's makes the mapping from human task demonstrations to the robot's actions more direct, reducing the gap and making those demonstrations more useful for learning.
